content:
India's Supreme Court on Wednesday set aside an Allahabad High Court order that had directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED) to verify allegations that Congress leader Rahul Gandhi held assets disproportionate to his known sources of income, handing the Leader of the Opposition a significant legal reprieve.

A three-judge bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, sent the petition back to the High Court for a fresh hearing, ruling that the earlier orders could not stand because Gandhi had never been given a chance to be heard before they were passed. "All impugned orders passed by the High Court are set aside," the bench said, directing that the matter be placed before the Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court for the constitution of a fresh bench, which will begin proceedings afresh in open court.

The case began with a public interest petition filed by S Vignesh Shishir, a Karnataka-based BJP worker, who alleged that Gandhi's assets were disproportionate to his declared income and sought a probe by the CBI and the ED. On July 20, the Allahabad High Court directed the two agencies to verify the allegations. Gandhi challenged that order before the Supreme Court, and on August 17 the apex court barred the agencies from filing any report and told the High Court to defer the proceedings.

At the heart of the Supreme Court's ruling was a basic principle of natural justice: no order adverse to a person can be passed without giving that person an opportunity to respond. Senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for Gandhi, told the court that the High Court had adopted a process "completely unknown to law" — it had not even sought Gandhi's response and had permitted what he called a witch-hunt without questioning the petitioner's locus standi, or legal standing, to raise the issue through a writ petition.

The bench agreed that the question of maintainability was open, and it kept all contentions of both sides open for the fresh hearing, including whether such a petition can be entertained by a constitutional court at all. Crucially, it directed Shishir to implead Gandhi as a respondent in the writ petition, so that he can present his arguments against it. The court also turned down Shishir's request for in-camera proceedings, made on the ground that he feared for his life and safety, and insisted the matter be heard in open court.

The ruling is not a final judgment on the allegations themselves. The Supreme Court did not examine whether the claims about Gandhi's assets are true or false, and it did not grant Gandhi's separate plea to transfer the petition to another High Court or to the Supreme Court itself. As the Times of India noted, the CBI has not registered even a preliminary enquiry in the matter, and the complaint may yet prove wrong or right on the facts. What the court has decided is procedural: the probe cannot proceed on the basis of an order passed behind the respondent's back.

A separate petition filed by Shishir remains pending before the Allahabad High Court, in which he has sought criminal action against Gandhi alleging violations of citizenship laws, claiming the Congress leader held a British passport in addition to his Indian one. That matter was not before the Supreme Court on Wednesday.

The order came on a day of high political theatre in India, as the country marked the 77th Constitution Day. Prime Minister Narendra Modi used the occasion to attack the Congress over its record, including the Emergency, while the Congress organised nationwide Samvidhan Raksha Marches, raising concerns over alleged electoral irregularities and demanding accountability from the Election Commission, according to The Telegraph India. The court's intervention in the Gandhi case landed in the middle of that confrontation, and both sides were quick to read it through a political lens — Congress leaders presented it as a vindication of due process, while BJP voices insisted the underlying questions remain unanswered.

For Gandhi, who leads the opposition in the Lok Sabha, the practical effect is immediate: no federal agency is currently authorised to probe his assets under the Allahabad High Court's directions, and any future attempt will have to survive a hearing in which he is a party, with the maintainability of the petition itself in question. For the wider legal system, the case is a reminder that public interest litigation — a tool often used to target prominent politicians — must still clear the basic test of fairness before it can trigger an investigation.

The fresh bench in Allahabad will now decide, after hearing both sides, whether Shishir's petition is maintainable and whether any probe is warranted at all. Until then, the asset allegations against one of India's most prominent opposition leaders remain just that — allegations, untested in court. The episode also underscores a tension that runs through Indian public life: the use of courts and agencies as arenas of political contest, and the Supreme Court's role as the institution that keeps that contest within the bounds of procedure. As [The Telegraph India reported](https://www.telegraphindia.com/amp/india/rahul-asset-scan-bid-halted-supreme-court-orders-fresh-open-court-hearing-in-case-prnt/cid/2191292), the bench's message was plain — even in a case about a politician, the law must first hear the person it is about.

The ruling adds to a week of friction between New Delhi and Washington on trade, with India also facing new US tariff pressure — a separate front on which the government is still negotiating. [Read about the delayed India-US trade deal signing](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-us-trade-deal-signing-delayed-november-2026). Courts on both sides of the Atlantic have been busy this week: in the United States, a second federal judge blocked President Donald Trump's birthright citizenship order. [Read about that ruling here](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/second-judge-blocks-trump-birthright-citizenship-order-november-2026).
summary: India's Supreme Court has set aside an Allahabad High Court order directing the CBI and ED to probe allegations of disproportionate assets against Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, ruling he was never given a hearing and sending the case back for a fresh hearing in open court.
title: Supreme Court quashes order for CBI-ED probe into Rahul Gandhi's assets, orders fresh hearing
